title: Camus Writes to His Old Teacher
text:
Albert Camus grew up in a poor neighborhood of Algiers. His father had been killed in the First World War when Albert was a baby, and he was raised by his mother, who was partly deaf and could not read, and a stern grandmother. At primary school his teacher, Louis Germain, noticed the boy's gifts. He gave him extra lessons for free, prepared him for the scholarship exam for the lycee, and went to his home to persuade his family to let him continue school instead of going out to work.

In October 1957 Camus learned he had won the Nobel Prize in Literature, at only forty three. On November 19 he sat down and wrote to Germain. He told his old teacher that when he heard the news, his first thought after his mother was of him. Without the affectionate hand Germain had extended to the poor little child he had been, and without his teaching and example, none of it would have happened. The honor, he wrote, gave him a chance to tell Germain what he had been and still was for him.

Germain answered with a long, moving letter. Camus dedicated his Nobel lecture to him. The letters were later published with his unfinished autobiographical novel, The First Man.
lesson: Tell the people who helped you early on what they meant to you, especially at your moments of success. They rarely know, and it may mean everything to them.
source: Albert Camus, letter to Louis Germain, November 19, 1957, published in Le Premier Homme (The First Man, 1994)
